title: Białystok’s Textile Economy and Jewish Workers
summary: Industry and labor shaped the city’s prosperity and the everyday lives of many Jewish residents, making them essential to understanding Bialystok beyond its political history.
editorialContent:
![Białystok, the industrial city remembered by its Jewish community](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Bazylika_w_Bia%C5%82ymstoku_-_Emilia_Ernst.jpg/1920px-Bazylika_w_Bia%C5%82ymstoku_-_Emilia_Ernst.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A textile city beside Łódź

The memorial book remembers [Białystok](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_1fd067a7479a54f5797bfb15) as a city whose Jewish life was bound up with textile production. It places the city among major industrial centers, comparing its output with Moscow and [Łódź](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_e96a4906e40b6045a70a7966). That comparison is a measure of civic pride as well as commerce: Białystok’s Jews were not simply participants in an industry elsewhere, but manufacturers, skilled workers and organizers in a town whose fortunes increasingly turned on cloth.

The wider history helps explain why the comparison mattered. Białystok grew into an industrial center in the nineteenth century, while Łódź became a much larger textile city. The memorial book’s claim that Białystok ranked third after Moscow and Łódź—and later surpassed Łódź in certain kinds of fabric and blankets—is its own account of the town’s standing, not an independently verified league table. An overview of Jewish Białystok likewise connects the city’s nineteenth-century growth to textile manufacture and reports that, by 1867, Jews owned about half of its 89 weaving factories. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Bia%C5%82ystok?utm_source=openai))

## Steam power, and who could use it

The memorial book marks a turning point around 1850, when [Nahum Mints](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_3a68ae90b4828b8dfa071e6f) and [Sender Bloch](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_6c8ac21293827d1933e3c766) introduced steam looms among Białystok’s manufacturers. In its account, that change began a longer transition from hand weaving toward mechanized production. The names matter: industrial modernization here was not an abstraction, but a decision made by local Jewish manufacturers whose work helped shape the city’s industrial future.

The book’s other testimony, however, complicates any simple story of machines bringing progress to everyone. One account says steam-powered equipment was monopolized by German, Polish and Russian owners, leaving Jewish workers confined largely to hand looms even as factories changed around them. It also describes unemployment and hardship among textile workers. The accounts do not fully resolve how widely or quickly Jewish manufacturers adopted the new machinery; they preserve instead the unevenness of change, in which ownership, access to capital and workers’ livelihoods did not move in step. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Bialystok1/bia020.html?utm_source=openai))

A technical-school memoir in the memorial book offers a different angle on mechanization: students learned to operate steam looms and study woven patterns, as well as dyeing, finishing and preparing yarn. The machinery connected local production to wider industrial knowledge and imported equipment. But technical skill did not erase the divisions between owners and workers, or between those with access to modern machines and those still dependent on handwork. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Bialystok5/bia036.html?utm_source=openai))

## Manufacturers, families and civic life

The memorial book names manufacturers who made the industry visible in daily life. Among them were [Dodje Zabludovsky](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_1cd41631839d767286f96a45), [Nakh-Dovid Bloch](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_481b720a9f29a53dcd6810b4), and the [Freidkin brothers](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_58d2b11e658b0bd76b4dff0f), associated with a cloth factory, and [Krinsky brothers](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_d55c02c1c88ccc854ca51d7f), identified with a dye business. The book also associates these families with the Jewish Sports Club, suggesting that industrial and commercial circles were part of the broader network of Jewish communal life.

Sender Bloch’s recorded connection to the [Jewish Hospital in Białystok](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_863a8fc296b108a0d4c6c363), which the book says he founded, points to another dimension of economic standing: manufacturers could become civic benefactors as well as employers. The connected record also names his wife, [Malka Raizel Bloch](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_d63dce21ff725aa3bc5ba757), but the material available here does not establish more about her role in the business or hospital. The memorial book’s brief entries preserve the ties; further family and institutional records would be needed to reconstruct them fully.

The business world was not confined to Białystok. The book invokes [Abraham Jacob](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_0106385ada2a75b79b7fe5c3), a textile manufacturer in Łódź and uncle of Meir Walach, as well as people who came from or worked in Łódź. Such connections remind us that the two cities belonged to overlapping networks of migration, trade and work. The record does not, by itself, tell us how goods, capital or family members moved between them.

## Workers organize and strike

The most direct memorial-book account of a labor dispute is the strike by [seventy Jewish weavers](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_b121e595cc580af4b0fcc9f6) against factory owner Aharon Surazki. The supplied record gives no date, but another chapter of the same memorial book places the stoppage in 1882 and describes the workers’ demand for higher wages. Its account says many strikers were Hasidim who worshipped in the same religious circle as Surazki. The conflict thus unfolded across a boundary that was at once economic and intimate: employer and workers shared a religious world, but not the same material interests. The book remembers the strike as an early labor action, not as proof that religious fellowship prevented workplace conflict. ([jewishgen.org](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Bialystok1/biay009.html?utm_source=openai))

That episode belonged to a larger workers’ movement. The memorial book describes labor exchanges, political debate and repeated strikes, while placing textile workers among the people who helped make Białystok a center of Jewish labor politics. A broader account of Białystok’s history also identifies the city as a major center of Jewish labor radicalism in the early twentieth century. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Bia%C5%82ystok?utm_source=openai)) These sources add context to the Surazki dispute, but do not make every later movement or party an outgrowth of that single strike.

The same book names [Eliezer Halberstam](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_ff5228ec84b9121e83e61947) among early textile workers and describes him elsewhere as an enlightened man and poet. His presence broadens the picture beyond owners and collective action: a working life could coexist with literary and intellectual engagement. The record does not supply a detailed employment history, so his precise trade and career remain uncertain.

## From livelihood to forced labor

The industry’s later history carries a devastating reversal. The same concentration of factories that had sustained employment and shaped civic identity became, under German occupation, a means of coercion. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum reports that most Jews confined in the Białystok ghetto were forced to work, primarily in large textile factories inside its boundaries. This is an independent historical account of wartime forced labor, not a continuation of the memorial book’s prewar workplace testimony. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/bialystok?utm_source=openai))

The broad arc is therefore not a tale of steady industrial progress. The memorial book remembers entrepreneurs, skilled workers, a hospital founder and weavers who challenged an employer over wages. Independent records place Białystok within the wider growth of Jewish textile enterprise and document the later exploitation of Jewish labor under Nazi rule. Between those histories lay not only changing machinery and markets, but a destruction of the community whose work had helped make the city an industrial center.
